raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man presented to the emergency department (ED) with a 10-day history of fever, 5 days of jaundice, and 3 days of altered consciousness. He had been hospitalized at another facility for a week, where tests for dengue, leptospirosis, scrub typhus, and typhoid were negative. His liver and kidney functions were abnormal, and his lipase levels were elevated. Hepatitis B and C serology were negative. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) imaging of the abdomen was reported to have multiple splenic infarcts. In this context, he was referred to as a case of acute undifferentiated febrile illness.
He had a continuous high-grade fever associated with chills and rigor for 10 days. Later, he developed a cough with expectoration, which was insidious in onset with whitish, nonblood-stained mucoid sputum. He also noticed yellowish discoloration of the eyes and urine 5 days after the fever onset. Seven days after the beginning of the fever, he developed altered sensorium in the form of reduced responsiveness and irrelevant talk. There was no history of seizures, vomiting, or chest pain. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus but was not taking his medications.
On presentation to the ED, he had a respiratory rate of 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 86%, pulse rate of 138 bpm, and blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. His saturation improved to 98% with oxygen via nasal prongs at 4 l/min. He was dehydrated, icteric, and had a tender splenomegaly. He was disoriented and had mild neck rigidity but no focal deficit. The rest of the system examination was unremarkable. His blood sugar was 385 mg/dl, and his urine ketones were negative. Acid-base analysis revealed metabolic acidosis with compensated respiratory alkalosis and type 1 respiratory failure with a P/F ratio of 217. Basic blood work showed a total leukocyte count of 4290/dL, abnormal renal function with hyperkalemia, elevated liver enzymes, and bilirubin [Table 1].
Blood cultures were taken while considering infective endocarditis or malaria as potential diagnoses. The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and antimalarials. A cardiac point-of-care ultrasound did not show any vegetation. Once the patient stabilized, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis was conducted. The scan revealed an enlarged spleen and multiple hypodense nonenhancing lesions in the liver and spleen, consistent with abscesses [Figures 1 and 2]. It also identified consolidation in the left posterior basal lung segment and small benign nodules in both lungs [Figure 3]. A separate brain CT scan showed no abnormalities. Based on the findings, meropenem was initiated for suspected melioidosis, and later blood cultures confirmed the presence of Burkholderia pseudomallei [Table 1]. Although the patient showed clinical improvement, he suffered a severe episode of hemoptysis on the 14th day of hospitalization and unfortunately passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old man presented with a 10-day history of fever, 5 days of jaundice, and 3 days of altered consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced continuous high-grade fever with chills and rigor for 10 days, followed by an insidious cough productive of whitish, non-blood-stained mucoid sputum. Five days after fever onset, he noticed yellowish discoloration of his eyes and urine, and at day 7 he developed altered sensorium characterized by reduced responsiveness and irrelevant talk. He had been hospitalized at an outside facility for 1 week for acute undifferentiated febrile illness, where testing for dengue, leptospirosis, scrub typhus, typhoid, and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative, liver and kidney function tests were abnormal, lipase was elevated, and an abdominal contrast-enhanced CT was reported as showing multiple splenic infarcts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, but was non-adherent and not taking any antidiabetic medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, rigor, productive cough with whitish mucoid sputum, scleral icterus, dark urine, and altered sensorium (reduced responsiveness and irrelevant talk). Negative for seizures, vomiting, or chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: On ED presentation: respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 86% on room air (improving to 98% on 4 L/min oxygen via nasal prongs), pulse rate 138 bpm, and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. General and systemic exam showed dehydration, icterus, tender splenomegaly, disorientation, and mild neck rigidity without focal neurological deficits. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood glucose was 385 mg/dL with negative urine ketones. Arterial acid-base analysis showed metabolic acidosis with compensated respiratory alkalosis and type 1 respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 217). Basic blood work revealed total leukocyte count of 4290/dL, abnormal renal function with hyperkalemia, and elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. Cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) showed no valvular vegetations.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated splenomegaly, multiple hypodense non-enhancing lesions in the liver and spleen consistent with visceral abscesses, consolidation in the left posterior basal lung segment, and small benign bilateral lung nodules. Non-contrast CT scan of the brain showed no abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated septicemic melioidosis with bilateral pulmonary involvement and multiple hepatic and splenic abscesses, confirmed by blood cultures isolating Burkholderia pseudomallei (infective endocarditis, malaria, dengue, leptospirosis, scrub typhus, typhoid, and viral hepatitis B/C were ruled out). Management and clinical course: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and antimalarials were initiated on admission, and therapy was switched to intravenous meropenem following CT demonstration of hepatosplenic abscesses. Despite initial clinical improvement on meropenem, the patient suffered a severe episode of hemoptysis on day 14 of hospitalization and died.
